title: Simple Record-Keeping (Visual & Practical)
subtitle: Keep clear daily records of sales, expenses, stock, credit and cash in a notebook or on your phone, and use them to know your real profit.
description: A hands-on course for market traders and small business owners, including those with limited schooling. You will set up a simple notebook (or picture book) with a sales book, expenses page, stock cards, debtors list and cash book, then use them to calculate profit, plan stock and prepare for loans. Every lesson has worked examples in naira and a practice task you do in your own business.
outcomes: Record every sale and expense on the day it happens, in a notebook, picture book or phone
Keep stock cards and a debtors list that reveal missing goods and unpaid credit
Balance a cash book daily for both cash and bank or wallet money
Pay yourself a fixed drawing and keep business money separate
Calculate monthly gross and net profit using stock counts
Prepare a simple record pack for a loan, grant or partner
audience: Women market traders and small business owners in Nigeria and across Africa who want simple, practical records, whatever their level of schooling.
tools: An exercise book (60 to 120 leaves), biro and ruler
A simple calculator or the phone calculator
An envelope or folder for receipts
Optional: a smartphone with the free Google Sheets app and a Google account

modules.title: Why records matter
modules.overview: Records are the written memory of your business. In this module you learn what a record is, the five things every small trader should write down, what goes wrong when nothing is written, and how to choose between a notebook and a phone.

lessons.title: What a business record is, and why every trader needs one
objectives: Explain in one sentence what a business record is
Name the people who use a trader's records
Tell the difference between business money and profit
Start a simple first page in a notebook

blocks.text: A **business record** is anything written down that shows what happened in your business: a sale, a purchase, money you paid out, goods you gave on credit, money that came in by transfer. It can be a line in a notebook, a receipt, a POS slip, or an entry in a phone app. The important thing is that it is **written at the time it happens**, so you do not need to remember it later.

blocks.name: taking-notes
blocks.alt: A woman writing notes in a book
blocks.caption: Writing it down at the moment it happens is the whole secret of record-keeping.

blocks.text: Many market traders keep everything in their head. That works when you sell one product to a few people. It stops working when you have ten products, five customers buying on credit, two suppliers, school fees to pay and a POS agent sending transfers. The head forgets, mixes things up, and remembers the good days more than the bad ones. Paper and phones do not forget.
Who uses your records?

items: **You**, to know if you are really making money and which goods sell best.
**Your family or a helper**, so the shop can run when you are sick or travelling.
**Your cooperative, esusu group or microfinance bank**, when you ask for a loan.
**A business partner or supplier**, who wants to see that you pay and sell steadily.
**A grant or training programme**, which often asks how much you sell in a month.

blocks.text: Money in your hand is not the same as profit

This is the most important idea in the whole course. At the end of a busy day you may have a lot of cash in your bag. But part of that money must go back to buy new stock. Part of it pays for transport, market levy and the boy who helps you carry loads. Only what is left after all those costs is **profit**. Without records you cannot see the difference, and many traders end up spending their capital (the money that runs the business) thinking it is profit.

blocks.title: How a record becomes a decision
items: Something happens
Write it down
Add up weekly
See the pattern
Make a decision
blocks.caption: Each sale or cost you write becomes part of a total, and totals show you what to do next.

blocks.title: Worked example: Bisi's pepper stall, one day
blocks.context: For example, Bisi sells fresh pepper and tomatoes in a Lagos market. She buys from a supplier in the morning and sells all day. Amounts are approximate.
steps: She buys a basket of tomatoes for about ₦18,000 and a bag of pepper for about ₦12,000. Total stock bought: ₦30,000.
She pays transport of about ₦2,000 and market ticket of about ₦500.
By evening she counts ₦38,000 in her bag.
Without a record she thinks: "I made ₦38,000 today."
With a record she calculates: ₦38,000 minus ₦30,000 stock minus ₦2,500 costs = ₦5,500.
blocks.result: Bisi's real profit for the day is about ₦5,500, not ₦38,000. If she spends ₦10,000 on household things tonight, she has eaten into the money she needs to buy tomorrow's stock.

blocks.title: Start with a cheap notebook
blocks.text: You do not need to buy anything special. A 40 or 60 leaf exercise book, a biro and a ruler are enough to begin. Draw lines with the ruler so each page has columns.
What makes a good record

items: **Dated**: every page and every line has the date.
**Complete**: every sale and every cost, even small ones like ₦200 sachet water for customers.
**Honest**: write what really happened, not what you wish happened.
**Kept safe**: away from rain, children and rats, in a nylon bag or a box.
**Easy to read**: one line for one thing, numbers written clearly.

blocks.text: If you cannot read or write well, you can still keep records. Use pictures or symbols for each product (a drawing of a tomato, a bottle, a bag of rice), use tally marks for each item sold, and ask a trusted child or friend to write the totals at night. Some traders send a WhatsApp voice note to themselves after each sale and write it down in the evening. The method matters less than doing it every day.

A simple first page needs only a few things: the **date** at the top, a column for **what happened** ("sold 3 tins of tomato paste" or "paid keke"), a column for **money in** and a column for **money out**. At the bottom of the day, draw a line and write the two totals. Do not worry about neat handwriting. A page full of honest, untidy numbers is far more useful than a beautiful empty book.

Record-keeping is also not the same as accounting. Accountants prepare formal statements for big companies. What you need is simpler: a clear daily list of money in, money out, goods in and goods out. That simple list is enough to answer the big questions: Am I making profit? Which goods should I buy more of? Who owes me? Can I afford this loan?

takeaways: A record is something written at the time it happens
Cash in your bag is not profit
Profit is what is left after stock and all costs
Records help you, your family, lenders and partners
Pictures, tally marks and helpers work if reading is hard

activity.title: Set up your first record page
steps: Get an exercise book, a biro and a ruler.
On page one write your business name, what you sell and today's date.
Draw three columns: What happened, Money in, Money out.
For one full day, write every sale and every cost as it happens.
At night, add the Money in column and the Money out column.
activity.evidence: A photo of your first full day page with both totals written at the bottom

lessons.title: The five things to record: sales, expenses, stock, credit and cash
objectives: List the five core records of a small business
Match each record to the question it answers
Decide which records your own business needs first
Set up one notebook with five sections

blocks.text: Think of your records as the **memory of your business**. A good memory answers questions quickly. When a customer says "I have paid you", your memory should show if she did. When your supplier raises prices, your memory should show what you paid last month. There are five records that answer almost every question a small trader has.

blocks.name: ledger
blocks.caption: One book, divided into sections, can hold all five records.

blocks.text: The five core records

head: Record
What you write
Question it answers
rows: Each sale: date, item, quantity, price, cash or transfer
How much did I sell today, this week, this month?
Each cost: date, what for, amount
Goods bought in, goods sold, goods left
What do I have left, and what is missing?
Who took goods on credit, how much, when they promised to pay
Who owes me and how much?
All money in and all money out, with a running balance
How much money should I have right now?

blocks.title: The five records work together
items: Buy stock
Sell goods
Record cash or credit
Pay expenses
Count what is left
blocks.caption: Every trading day goes round this cycle, and each step has its own record.

blocks.text: How they connect

These records are not separate worlds. When you sell a bag of rice for cash, it goes in your **sales record**, your **stock** goes down by one bag, and your **cash book** goes up. When you sell the same bag on credit, sales and stock still change, but instead of the cash book you write it in your **debtors list**. When the customer pays later, the debtors list goes down and the cash book goes up. When you pay a bus driver to carry goods, that is an **expense** and the cash book goes down.

blocks.title: Worked example: Ngozi's provisions shop, three transactions
blocks.context: For example, Ngozi runs a small provisions shop in Enugu. Prices are approximate.
steps: Morning: she sells 2 tins of milk at about ₦1,200 each for cash. Sales record: +₦2,400. Stock of milk: down 2 tins. Cash book: +₦2,400.

Afternoon: Mama Chidi takes a carton of noodles worth about ₦9,500 and promises to pay on Friday. Sales record: +₦9,500. Stock of noodles: down 1 carton. Debtors list: Mama Chidi owes ₦9,500, due Friday.
Evening: Ngozi pays ₦1,500 for a keke to bring new goods. Expenses record: transport ₦1,500. Cash book: minus ₦1,500.
End of day: sales total ₦11,900. Cash book movement: +₦2,400 minus ₦1,500 = +₦900. Debtors: ₦9,500 owed.
blocks.result: Ngozi sold ₦11,900 of goods but only ₦900 more cash is in her hand. Her records explain exactly why, so she will not panic or accuse anyone.

blocks.text: Which records to start with

If five records feel like too much, start with two: the **sales record** and the **expenses record**. These alone let you work out a rough profit. Add the **debtors list** the very first time someone buys on credit, because credit is where traders lose the most money. Add the **stock record** when you have more than a few products. Add the **cash book** when you are ready to check your cash every day.

blocks.title: Keep receipts too
blocks.text: A record is not only what you write. Supplier receipts, POS slips, bank alerts and transfer screenshots are also records. Keep paper receipts in an envelope for each month and write the month on the front. On your phone, make a photo album called "Shop receipts".
Setting up one notebook for everything

items: Take a 120 leaf notebook if you can, or two smaller ones.
Count the pages and divide them: sales and expenses (half the book), stock (a quarter), debtors (a few pages), cash book (the rest).
Stick a small piece of paper or tape on the edge of each section so you can open it fast.
Write the section name at the top of its first page in big letters.
Rule columns on the first page of each section before you start.

blocks.text: Write every amount in naira without the kobo, and always put the date in the same style, for example 05/10 for 5 October. Use the same name for each product every time, such as "Rice 50kg bag" rather than "rice" one day and "big bag" the next. Small habits like these make adding up much easier at the end of the week, and they let a helper or family member read your book without asking you questions.

Many traders also keep a separate small book only for credit, because they carry it around to show customers what they owe. That is fine, as long as you check it against your main records every week. In the coming lessons you will learn exactly what columns each section needs and how to total them.

takeaways: Five records: sales, expenses, stock, debtors, cash book
One transaction can touch two or three records
Start with sales and expenses, add credit immediately when it happens
Receipts and bank alerts are records too

activity.title: Divide your notebook
steps: Pick a notebook for your business only.
Mark five sections with tape or paper tabs.
Write the section names and rule the columns for each.
Write three real transactions from today into every section they touch.
activity.evidence: Photo of the five tabbed sections and the three transactions

lessons.title: What it costs you when nothing is written down
objectives: Recognise five common money leaks in a business without records
Estimate how much a small daily leak costs in a year
Explain how records protect relationships with customers and family
Identify one leak in your own business

blocks.text: Traders rarely lose money in one big disaster. Most money leaks out quietly, ₦200 here, ₦1,000 there, a forgotten debt, a helper who "borrows" from the drawer. Each leak looks small. Over a year they can be the difference between a growing shop and one that cannot restock.

blocks.name: empty-wallet
blocks.caption: Small unrecorded leaks are how a busy shop ends up with an empty purse.

blocks.text: Five common leaks

items: **Forgotten credit.** A customer takes goods and you forget, or you remember a smaller amount than she really owes.
**Eating the capital.** You spend sales money on the house, not knowing part of it was money to restock.
**Selling below cost.** Your supplier raised the price and you did not notice, so you now sell at a loss.
**Missing stock.** Goods are stolen, spoiled or taken by family, and nobody knows how many.
**Untracked small expenses.** Transport, levies, phone data, nylon bags, change for customers. Each is small, together they are large.

blocks.title: How small leaks build up
items: ₦500 a day
₦3,000 a week
₦13,000 a month
blocks.caption: A leak of about ₦500 a day, six days a week, becomes a very large sum in a year.

blocks.title: Worked example: how much a daily leak really costs
blocks.context: For example, Amina sells drinks and snacks at a motor park and does not record small giveaways and unpaid snacks. Amounts are approximate.
steps: She guesses she loses about ₦500 a day to snacks given on credit that are never paid, and things taken by children.
She works 6 days a week: ₦500 × 6 = ₦3,000 a week.
There are about 52 weeks in a year: ₦3,000 × 52 = ₦156,000.
One crate of soft drinks costs her about ₦6,000, so ₦156,000 is about 26 crates of stock.
blocks.result: A leak she thinks is "nothing" costs her about ₦156,000 a year, enough to buy around 26 crates. Writing it down is the first step to stopping it.

blocks.text: When the supplier raises the price

Prices of goods in Nigerian markets can change quickly. If you buy a bag of sugar for one price this month and a higher price next month, but keep selling at your old price, your profit shrinks or disappears. Without a record of what you paid, you may not notice for weeks. With a record, you see the new cost the same day and can adjust your selling price or buy elsewhere.
Records protect relationships

Arguments over money damage businesses and families. A customer says she paid; you say she did not. Your husband thinks the shop makes plenty; you know it does not. A helper is accused of stealing when the real problem is spoiled goods. A written, dated record settles these arguments calmly. You can show the page instead of raising your voice. When a customer sees you write her credit in front of her and read it back, she is also less likely to dispute it later.

blocks.title: Watch for scams on transfers
blocks.text: Some people show a fake transfer screen or a fake SMS alert and walk away with goods. Before you release goods, check that the money has entered your own account in your bank or wallet app (for example Opay, Moniepoint or your bank app), not just the customer's phone. Record the transfer only after you confirm it.
What records cannot do

Records do not make money by themselves. They show you the truth, and the truth is sometimes uncomfortable: a product you love may be losing money, or a relative may be taking more than you thought. The value comes from acting on what you see. In Module 4 you will learn how to read your records and turn them into decisions.
Stock that walks away

Goods leave a shop in many ways besides sales. Tomatoes spoil in the heat. A child takes a biscuit. A relative collects a bag of rice "for the house". A helper gives a friend a discount you did not agree. None of this is a problem if it is written: you can decide what is fair and what must stop. It becomes a problem only when nobody knows. A simple stock count at the end of each week, compared with what your sales record says you sold, shows you how much stock disappeared without a sale.

Also remember that goods you take for your own family are a real cost to the business. If you take a carton of noodles home, write it down as "taken for home" at what you paid for it. That way your profit figure stays honest, and you can see how much the household is really drawing from the shop each month.

takeaways: Money usually leaks slowly, not in one disaster
A ₦500 daily leak can cost about ₦156,000 a year
Records reveal price rises before they eat your profit
A written record settles arguments calmly
Always confirm transfers in your own account before releasing goods

activity.title: Find one leak
steps: Think about the last month and list every way money or goods may have left without being written.
Estimate the amount for each leak per day or week.
Multiply to find the cost for a year.
Choose the one record from this lesson that would catch your biggest leak.

lessons.title: Notebook, picture book or phone: choosing your method
objectives: Compare paper and phone record-keeping honestly
Choose a method that fits your reading level, phone and budget
Design a picture-based record if reading is difficult
Set a daily time for writing records

blocks.text: There is no single right method. The best method is the one you will actually use every day. Some traders do perfectly with an exercise book for twenty years. Others prefer a phone because it adds up for them. Some use both: a notebook in the stall during the day, and a phone summary at night.

blocks.name: personal-notebook
blocks.alt: A person with an open notebook
blocks.caption: A notebook is cheap, needs no data and never runs out of battery.

blocks.text: Paper or phone?

blocks.title: Paper notebook versus phone
items: Paper notebook
Phone
blocks.caption: Both work; choose based on your reading, phone and habits.
left: Can get wet, torn or lost
right: Can back up to the cloud
Phone can be stolen or broken

blocks.text: Option 1: the ruled notebook

This is the classic method. You rule columns with a ruler and write each transaction on one line. It suits anyone who can read and write numbers. Use a pen, not a pencil, so entries cannot be rubbed out. If you make a mistake, draw one line through it and write the correct figure next to it; do not tear out pages.
Option 2: the picture and tally book

If reading is hard for you, draw a small picture for each product at the top of a column: a loaf of bread, a bottle of oil, a sachet of water. Each time you sell one, make a tally mark (four lines and a fifth across). Use a coloured pen for credit sales, for example red. At night, count the tallies and multiply by the price, or ask someone you trust to do it with you.

blocks.title: Worked example: Kemi's picture tally for bread
blocks.context: For example, Kemi sells bread and cannot write easily. She sells small loaves at about ₦700 and big loaves at about ₦1,500. Prices are approximate.
steps: She draws a small loaf on the left of the page and a big loaf on the right.
Each sale gets one tally mark under the right picture. Credit sales are marked in red.
At night she counts: small loaf 23 marks (3 in red), big loaf 11 marks (1 in red).
Credit (red): 3 × ₦700 + 1 × ₦1,500 = ₦2,100 + ₦1,500 = ₦3,600, so cash she should have from sales is ₦32,600 minus ₦3,600 = ₦29,000.
blocks.result: With only pictures and marks, Kemi knows she sold about ₦32,600 of bread, should have about ₦29,000 cash, and is owed ₦3,600.

blocks.text: Option 3: the phone

A smartphone can hold your records in a free spreadsheet such as **Google Sheets**, or in a bookkeeping app downloaded from the Google Play Store or App Store. A spreadsheet adds totals for you and saves a copy online if you sign in with a Google account. Before choosing any app, check that it is free or affordable, works offline, lets you export or back up your data, and has good recent reviews. In Module 4 you will set one up step by step.

blocks.title: Protect your phone records
blocks.text: If you keep records on a phone, set a screen lock (PIN or fingerprint). Never share your bank PIN or one-time codes with anyone, including people who say they are from a bank or app. Back up regularly so a lost phone does not mean lost records.
Make it a habit

items: Choose one fixed time each day to finish your records, for example after closing and before going home.
Keep the notebook and pen in the same place every day.
Write small things immediately; do the adding up at your fixed time.
Once a week, on the same day, add up the whole week.
Show your records to someone you trust once a month so you stay accountable.

blocks.text: Mixing methods sensibly

Many traders get the best of both. During a busy market day, phones are awkward: your hands are full, the screen is hard to see in the sun, and you worry about theft. So write quickly in a small notebook or on a tally sheet, then type the day's totals into your phone in the evening. The notebook is your **original record**; the phone is your **summary and backup**. Keep the notebooks for at least a year, because lenders or partners may want to see them.

Whatever you choose, keep the same layout every day. If your columns move around, totals become confusing and mistakes hide. Copy the column headings onto every new page, or in a phone, keep using the same sheet with the same headings.

head: If this is you...
Try this method
rows: Reads and writes numbers, no smartphone
Picture and tally book, with a helper at night
Has a smartphone and some data
Notebook in the day, Google Sheets at night
Notebook plus phone spreadsheet or app

takeaways: The best method is the one you use every day
Use pen, not pencil, and never tear out pages
Pictures and tally marks work well for low literacy
Phones add up for you but need a lock and backups
Fix one daily time for records

modules.title: Sales, stock and credit records
modules.overview: This module builds the records that track what you sell and what you are owed. You will set up a daily sales book, total it into daily and weekly summaries, count your stock so missing goods show up, and keep a debtors list that gets your money back.

lessons.title: The daily sales book: recording every sale
objectives: Rule a sales book with the right columns
Record cash, transfer and credit sales correctly
Group many small sales without losing accuracy
Check the day's sales against cash and transfers received

blocks.text: Your **sales book** is the most used page in your business. Every time goods leave your hands in exchange for money, or for a promise of money, it gets a line. If you only keep one record, keep this one. It tells you how much you sell, what sells, and on which days.

blocks.name: business-shop
blocks.alt: A trader at a shop counter
blocks.caption: Every sale at your counter gets one line in the sales book.

blocks.text: The columns you need

The prices in this table are only for illustration and are approximate. The **Paid by** column is very important. Today most Nigerian traders receive money three ways: **cash**, **transfer or POS** (into a bank or wallet such as Moniepoint, Opay or a commercial bank), and **credit** (the customer will pay later). Marking each sale lets you check each type separately at night.

blocks.title: Recording one sale
items: Customer buys
Confirm payment
Write the line
Note cash, transfer or credit
Total at closing
blocks.caption: Payment is confirmed before the line is written, and every line says how it was paid.

blocks.text: When you are too busy to write each sale

A trader selling sachet water or roasted corn may make a hundred small sales an hour. Writing each one is not realistic. Instead, use a **tally**: one column per product, one mark per item sold. Or count stock at opening and closing (you will learn this in lesson 3) and let the difference tell you how many were sold. Write larger sales, credit sales and transfers as single lines, because those are the ones people argue about.

blocks.title: Worked example: Funke's sales book for one morning
blocks.context: For example, Funke sells foodstuff in Ibadan. She writes each larger sale and tallies small items. Prices are approximate.
steps: Garri, 1 paint bucket at about ₦3,500: 4 sold for cash. 4 × ₦3,500 = ₦14,000 cash.
Beans, 1 paint bucket at about ₦5,000: 2 sold by transfer. 2 × ₦5,000 = ₦10,000 transfer.
Crayfish small cups at about ₦500: 12 tally marks, all cash. 12 × ₦500 = ₦6,000 cash.
Palm oil, 1 bottle at about ₦2,500: 1 to Iya Sade on credit. ₦2,500 credit.
Totals: cash ₦14,000 + ₦6,000 = ₦20,000. Transfer ₦10,000. Credit ₦2,500. All sales ₦32,500.
blocks.result: Funke's morning sales were about ₦32,500. She should have ₦20,000 more cash in her purse, ₦10,000 more in her account, and Iya Sade should be in her debtors list for ₦2,500.

blocks.text: Checking at closing time

items: Add the Total column for the whole day.
Add the cash sales only. Count your cash. Subtract the float (the change money you started with). The difference should equal cash sales.
Open your bank or wallet app. Add today's incoming transfers. They should equal transfer sales.
Check that every credit sale also appears in your debtors list.
If something does not match, write the difference and a short note (for example "₦500 short, maybe wrong change").

blocks.title: Use your bank alerts
blocks.text: Your bank or wallet app keeps a history of every transfer you receive. At closing, scroll through today's credits and tick each one against a transfer line in your sales book. Unmatched alerts often mean you forgot to write a sale.

Do not expect a perfect match every day. Small differences happen from wrong change or a sale you forgot. What matters is that you notice them. If you are short by a few hundred naira once a month, that is normal. If you are short almost every day, something is wrong: a pricing mistake, a helper's error, or theft. Your sales book is how you find out.
Returns and discounts

Sometimes a customer brings goods back, or you give a discount to close a sale. Write these honestly. For a return, write a new line with the item and the amount in brackets, for example (2,800), and take it away from the day's total. For a discount, write the price you actually received, not the shelf price. If you write the shelf price, your sales book will say you earned more than you did, and your cash will never match.

If a helper sells for you, ask her to use the same book and the same columns. At closing, go through the lines together. This is not about suspicion; it is how both of you can prove the shop's money is correct.

At the end of each page, write the page total at the bottom and carry it to the top of the next page as "brought forward". This way, the last page of the day shows the full day's total without you adding every page again.

takeaways: One line per sale: date, item, quantity, price, total, how paid
Mark every sale as cash, transfer or credit
Tally very small sales instead of writing each
At closing, check cash and transfers against the book
Note differences, do not hide them

activity.title: Run a full sales book day
steps: Rule a page with the six columns shown.
Count your float (starting change) and write it at the top.
Record every sale for one full day, tallying small items.
At closing, total cash, transfer and credit separately.
Check cash against your purse and transfers against your app, and write any difference.
activity.evidence: Photo of the completed day's page with the three totals and your check notes

lessons.title: Daily and weekly sales summaries
objectives: Produce a one-line daily summary from your sales book
Build a weekly summary table
Spot your best and worst days and products
Calculate an average daily sale

blocks.text: A sales book full of lines is useful, but you cannot see the big picture in it. A **summary** squeezes each day into one line and each week into one small table. With summaries, patterns appear: Saturday is your best day, oil sells more at month end, rainy days are slow. These patterns guide when to buy stock and when to stay open longer.

blocks.name: data-table
blocks.alt: A person looking at a table of figures
blocks.caption: A summary turns pages of sales lines into one small table you can read in a minute.

blocks.text: The daily summary line

At the end of each day, after checking your sales book, write one line in a separate **summary page**: the date, total sales, cash, transfer, credit, and one short note about the day (rain, market day, festival, you closed early). The note is what helps you explain the numbers later.
The weekly summary table

These figures are illustrative and approximate. Check the table: each day's cash plus transfer plus credit must equal its total, and the WEEK row is the sum of each column. If the week row does not balance, there is an adding mistake somewhere; find it before you trust the numbers.

blocks.title: From sale to monthly picture
items: Each sale
Daily total
Weekly table
Monthly total
Compare months
blocks.caption: Each level adds up the level before it, so a mistake in one sale affects everything above it.

blocks.title: Worked example: what the week tells Halima
blocks.context: For example, Halima uses the weekly table above for her provisions stall in Kano. Amounts are approximate.
steps: Week total: ₦188,000 over 6 days. Average per day: ₦188,000 ÷ 6 = about ₦31,333.
Best day: Saturday at ₦48,000. Worst day: Thursday at ₦22,500 (rain).
Transfers are ₦70,000 out of ₦188,000. ₦70,000 ÷ ₦188,000 = about 0.37, so roughly 37 out of every 100 naira came by transfer.
Credit is ₦12,000. ₦12,000 ÷ ₦188,000 = about 0.06, so about 6 out of every 100 naira is not yet paid.
blocks.result: Halima decides to restock on Friday so she is full for Saturday, keep her POS and transfer details clearly displayed since many customers pay that way, and keep credit at or below this level.

blocks.text: Product summaries

Once a week, also count how many of each main product you sold. You do not need every item, just your top five or six. A simple table with product names down the side and days across the top, filled with quantities, will quickly show which goods move fast and which sit on the shelf. Fast movers deserve more space and more stock. Slow movers tie up your money.

items: Fast mover: sells every day, runs out before restock. Buy a bit more next time.
Steady mover: sells most days. Keep the same quantity.
Slow mover: some days nothing sells. Buy less, or reduce price to clear it, or stop stocking it.
Seasonal: sells only at certain times (festive periods, school resumption). Stock up just before, not after.

blocks.title: Averages hide things
blocks.text: An average daily sale of about ₦31,000 does not mean every day is ₦31,000. Look at the best and worst days too. A very low day might be a warning (a new competitor nearby) or just rain.

Keep each week's summary on its own page, and at the end of the month add the four or five weekly totals into a **monthly total**. Compare months. Is this month higher or lower than last month? Why? Writing one sentence of explanation each month builds your understanding of your own market better than any training.

blocks.title: Worked example: comparing two months
blocks.context: For example, Halima adds up her weekly totals at month end. Amounts are approximate.
steps: Difference: ₦744,000 − ₦717,000 = ₦27,000 more in October.
Her notes show the ₦160,000 week had three days of heavy rain.
blocks.result: Sales grew by about ₦27,000 even with a rainy week. Halima writes: "October up, rain week low, Saturday still strongest."

blocks.text: If you use a phone, a spreadsheet is ideal for summaries because it adds columns automatically. But the habit matters more than the tool. Ten minutes on Saturday evening with a calculator and your notebook gives you the same picture.

takeaways: One summary line per day, one table per week
Cash plus transfer plus credit must equal total sales
Find your best and worst days and why
Count your top products weekly to find fast and slow movers
Add weeks into months and compare

activity.title: Build your weekly summary
steps: Using a week of your sales book, write one summary line per day.
Fill the weekly table with total, cash, transfer, credit and notes.
Check each row and the WEEK row add up correctly.
Work out your average daily sale and name your best and worst days.
Write one decision you will make from this week.
activity.evidence: Photo or copy of your weekly summary table with your average and one written decision

lessons.title: Stock records: what came in, what went out, what is left
objectives: Keep a stock card for each main product
Use opening stock, purchases and closing stock to find quantity sold
Detect missing stock by comparing counts with sales
Decide when to reorder

blocks.text: **Stock** (also called inventory) is the goods you have for sale. For most traders, stock is where most of the business money is sitting. A shop with ₦500,000 of goods on the shelves and ₦20,000 in the drawer has most of its money in stock. If stock is lost, spoiled or stolen and nobody notices, the business shrinks without anyone knowing why.

blocks.name: package
blocks.caption: Most of a trader's money sits in stock, so stock needs its own record.

blocks.text: The stock card

Give each main product its own page or card. The simplest stock card has these columns: **Date, In (bought), Out (sold or used), Balance (left)**. Every time you buy more, add to In. Every time you count or sell, reduce the balance. The balance on paper should match what you can physically count on the shelf.

In this illustration, the paper balance says 6 cartons but the physical count says 5. One carton is **missing**: maybe spoiled, given away, stolen, or sold and not written. Without a stock card, nobody would ever see it.

blocks.title: The stock formula
items: Opening stock
Plus purchases
Minus sold
Equals expected left
Compare with count
blocks.caption: Expected stock should equal counted stock; any gap needs an explanation.

blocks.text: The formula in words

**Opening stock + stock bought − stock sold = stock that should be left.** Count what is actually left. If it is less, the difference is a loss. You can also turn the formula around when you are too busy to record every sale: **opening stock + stock bought − closing stock = quantity that left the shop**. Compare that with your sales book.

blocks.title: Worked example: Esther's drinks
blocks.context: For example, Esther sells bottled soft drinks by the crate in Port Harcourt. Prices are approximate.
steps: Monday opening count: 10 crates. She buys 15 crates on Wednesday. Total available: 10 + 15 = 25 crates.
Saturday closing count: 7 crates. So 25 − 7 = 18 crates left the shop this week.
Her sales book shows 17 crates sold.
18 − 17 = 1 crate unexplained. One crate costs her about ₦6,000 to buy.
She asks her helper and learns 2 bottles broke and some were given to visitors without recording.
blocks.result: Esther loses about one crate a week, roughly ₦6,000 at cost. She now writes breakages and gifts in the Out column, and the gap disappears the next week.

blocks.text: When to reorder

Your stock card also tells you when to buy. Look at how much you sell in a normal week. If you sell about 14 cartons a week and your supplier takes 2 days to deliver, you need at least 4 cartons on hand when you order (14 ÷ 7 × 2 = 4), plus a little extra for busy days. Write this **reorder level** at the top of the card. When the balance drops to it, order.

blocks.title: Count at the same time each week
blocks.text: Choose one day and time, for example Saturday after closing, for a full stock count of your main products. Count when no customers are buying, and if possible have a second person count too.

items: Write breakages, spoilage and expired goods in the Out column with a note.
Write goods taken for home use in the Out column too.
Check expiry dates when counting; sell older stock first (first in, first out).
Store goods off the floor and away from water to reduce spoilage.

blocks.title: Expired goods
blocks.text: Do not sell food, drinks or medicines that are past their expiry date. Remove them, record them as spoiled, and learn from it by buying smaller quantities of that item next time.
Valuing your stock

Once a month, multiply each product's count by what you **paid** for it (not your selling price) and add them up. This is the value of your stock at cost. For example, 5 cartons of noodles at about ₦8,000 each is ₦40,000, and 7 crates of drinks at about ₦6,000 each is ₦42,000, so these two products alone hold ₦82,000 of your money. Knowing this figure matters when you calculate profit in Module 4 and when a lender asks how big your business is.

If your helper sells while you are away, a stock count before you leave and after you return is the fairest check for both of you. Write both counts on the card and sign them together. Disagreements become rare when the numbers are agreed on the spot.

You do not need a stock card for every tiny item. Start with your five most expensive or fastest moving products, since these carry the most money. Small items can be counted as a group, for example "sweets jar" or "seasoning cubes box".

takeaways: Stock is where most of your money sits
Opening + bought − sold = what should be left
Count weekly and compare with the card
Record breakages, spoilage and home use as Out
Set a reorder level from your weekly sales

activity.title: Stock card for your top product
steps: Choose your most valuable or fastest product.
Count it now and write the opening balance on a new card.
Record every purchase and every sale for one week.
Count again at the end of the week and compare with the card balance.
Write the gap, if any, and the most likely reason.
activity.evidence: Photo of the completed stock card with opening count, closing count and your explanation

lessons.title: The debtors list: tracking credit and getting paid
objectives: Keep a debtors list with dates and promised payment days
Record part-payments correctly
Set a simple credit limit for customers
Follow up debts politely using your records

blocks.text: Selling on credit ("pay me later", "I go pay Friday") keeps customers loyal, but it is also the fastest way for a small business to run out of money. Credit is stock that has left your shop with no money in return. Your **debtors list** is the record of everyone who owes you, how much, since when and when they promised to pay.

blocks.name: handshake
blocks.caption: Credit is built on trust, and a written debtors list protects that trust.

blocks.text: Columns for the debtors list

Figures are illustrative. Keep one page per regular customer, or one shared page with a line per debt. Write the debt **in front of the customer** and read it back to her: "Carton of noodles, ₦9,500, you will pay on the 10th." Some traders ask the customer to sign or thumbprint the line. This simple step prevents most disputes.

blocks.title: The credit cycle
items: Give goods
Write the debt
Remind on due date
Record payment
Update balance
blocks.caption: Every credit sale goes round this cycle until the balance reaches zero.

blocks.text: Part payments

Customers often pay a little at a time. Each time, write the date and amount paid, then the new balance. Never just cross out the old figure. When the debt is fully paid, write "PAID" and the date. At the same time, write the money received in your cash book (or note it as a transfer), because this is money coming in today even though the sale was earlier.

blocks.title: Worked example: Chioma's debtors at month end
blocks.context: For example, Chioma sells fabric in Aba and allows some regular customers credit. Amounts are approximate.
steps: Ada owes ₦25,000 from 2 weeks ago, promised last Friday. Not paid.
Joy owed ₦18,000, paid ₦10,000. Balance ₦8,000, promised next week.
Uche owes ₦40,000 from 7 weeks ago. Has stopped coming to the shop.
Her stock purchase for next week will cost about ₦120,000; she has ₦60,000 in hand.
blocks.result: Chioma is ₦60,000 short for restocking, and ₦73,000 is sitting with debtors. She calls Ada today, agrees a date with Joy, and stops further credit to Uche until the old debt is settled.

blocks.text: Age your debts

Once a week, sort your debtors by how long they have owed: under 1 week, 1 to 4 weeks, over 4 weeks. The longer a debt stays unpaid, the harder it is to collect. Concentrate your follow-up on the older debts before they become losses.
Set credit rules

items: **Who**: only regular customers you know well, with a working phone number.
**How much**: a limit per person, for example no more than one week's typical purchase.
**How long**: a clear payment date, usually within a week or two.
**One at a time**: no new credit until the last debt is paid, or at least reduced.
**Write it every time**: no credit sale without a line in the list.

blocks.title: A polite reminder message
blocks.text: On the due date, send a short WhatsApp or SMS: "Good morning Ma, this is Chioma from the fabric shop. A reminder that the balance of ₦8,000 is due today. Thank you for your custom." Being polite, specific and on time works better than waiting until you are angry.
Credit you owe to suppliers

Credit runs both ways. If your supplier gives you goods and you pay later, keep a separate page called **creditors** (people you owe), with the same columns: date, supplier, goods, amount, due date, paid, balance. Paying suppliers on time builds your reputation, and a supplier who trusts you may offer better prices or larger credit. Before you accept supplier credit, check from your sales summary that you will sell enough in time to pay.

blocks.title: Worked example: is ₦73,000 of debt a lot?
blocks.context: For example, Chioma compares her debts with her sales. Amounts are approximate.
steps: Her weekly sales are about ₦150,000.
Her debtors total ₦73,000.
₦73,000 ÷ ₦150,000 = about 0.49, so her customers owe her about half a week of sales.
blocks.result: Half a week of sales locked in credit is too much for a small shop that restocks weekly. Chioma sets a target of no more than about a quarter of a week's sales.

blocks.text: Some debts will never be paid. When you are sure a debt is lost, mark it "written off" with the date, so it stops making your list look better than it is. Treat it as a cost when you calculate profit. Then use the lesson: was the limit too high, or the customer unknown? Adjust your rules.

takeaways: Credit is stock that has left without money
Write every debt in front of the customer with a due date
Record part payments and the new balance each time
Sort debts by age and chase the oldest first
Set limits: who, how much, how long, one at a time

activity.title: Clean up your debtors list
steps: List everyone who owes you now, with amount and date of the debt.
Add a promised payment date for each, or agree one.
Sort them into under 1 week, 1 to 4 weeks, over 4 weeks.
Send polite reminders to anyone past their date.
Write your own credit rules (who, how much, how long) on the first page.
activity.evidence: Your updated debtors list with totals by age group and your written credit rules

quiz.q: Funke sold ₦20,000 for cash, ₦10,000 by transfer and ₦2,500 on credit. What are her total sales?
quiz.explain: Total sales include all three ways of paying: ₦20,000 + ₦10,000 + ₦2,500 = ₦32,500.

quiz.q: At closing, the cash sales in Funke's book are ₦20,000 but her purse, after removing the float, has ₦19,500. What should she do?
options: Write the ₦500 difference with a short note and watch for a pattern
quiz.explain: Small differences happen. Write them down honestly and watch whether they repeat; do not change the record to hide them.

quiz.q: Halima's weekly sales are ₦188,000 over 6 days. What is her average daily sale?
quiz.explain: Average = total ÷ number of days = ₦188,000 ÷ 6, about ₦31,333.

quiz.q: Esther had 10 crates, bought 15, and counted 7 at the end of the week. Her sales book shows 17 sold. How many crates are unexplained?
quiz.explain: 10 + 15 − 7 = 18 crates left the shop, but only 17 were recorded as sold, so 1 crate is unexplained.

quiz.q: Joy owed ₦18,000 and pays ₦10,000 today. What should Chioma write?
options: Paid ₦10,000, new balance ₦8,000, and record ₦10,000 in the cash book
Nothing until the full amount comes
quiz.explain: Record the part payment and new balance in the debtors list, and the money received in the cash book.

quiz.q: Which credit rule best protects a small trader?
options: Give credit to anyone who asks nicely
No new credit until the customer's last debt is paid or reduced
Never write debts down, it embarrasses customers
Let debts run as long as the customer keeps coming
quiz.explain: Limiting customers to one open debt at a time stops debts from piling up beyond what they can pay.

modules.title: Expenses and cash records
modules.overview: Here you track where money goes and check that the money you hold is right. You will record expenses in clear groups, keep a cash book with a running balance, separate business money from household money by paying yourself a fixed amount, and pull everything into weekly and monthly summaries.

lessons.title: Recording business expenses in clear groups
objectives: Record every business expense with date, purpose and amount
Separate stock purchases from running costs
Group expenses into a few simple categories
Keep receipts organised by month

blocks.text: An **expense** is any money the business pays out. For a trader there are two very different kinds. **Stock purchases** are goods you buy to sell again: bags of rice, cartons of noodles, bales of fabric. **Running costs** (also called operating expenses) are everything else you pay to keep trading: transport, shop rent, market levy, nylon bags, phone data, electricity, a helper's pay. Keep them in separate columns, because you treat them differently when calculating profit.

blocks.name: receipt
blocks.caption: Each receipt is proof of an expense; keep it with your records.

blocks.text: The expenses page

All figures are illustrative and approximate. Notice how the running costs for the day are small next to the stock purchase, but they still matter. Over a month they add up to a real sum, and if you do not record them you will think you are making more profit than you are.

blocks.title: Before you pay, check
items: Is this for the business?
Did I get a receipt?
Which category is it?
Have I written it down?
blocks.caption: Four quick questions make sure every business payment lands in your records.

blocks.text: Simple categories

items: **Stock**: goods for resale.
**Transport**: keke, okada, bus, loading and offloading.
**Rent and levies**: shop or stall rent, market ticket, association dues.
**Packaging**: nylon bags, paper, containers, labels.
**Phone and power**: data, airtime for business calls, electricity, fuel for a generator.
**Staff**: helper's pay, money for an apprentice's lunch.
**Other**: repairs, bank or POS charges, anything else.

blocks.text: Seven categories are enough for almost any trader. Use the same ones every week so you can compare. Bank transfer charges and POS fees are small, but they are real costs, so check your bank app and record them under Other.

blocks.title: Worked example: Rukayat's week of running costs
blocks.context: For example, Rukayat sells shoes at a Lagos market. She records running costs for one week. Amounts are approximate.
steps: Transport: ₦1,500 a day for 6 days = ₦9,000.
Market levy: ₦300 a day for 6 days = ₦1,800.
Nylon bags: 2 packs at ₦1,200 = ₦2,400.
Data for WhatsApp selling: ₦1,500.
Helper on Saturday: ₦3,000.
blocks.result: Rukayat's running costs are about ₦17,700 a week. Transport is the biggest at ₦9,000, so she looks for a cheaper way, such as sharing a keke with a neighbour trader.

blocks.text: Keeping receipts

items: Ask for a receipt for every business payment you can, especially stock purchases.
If there is no receipt (keke fare, for example), write the expense immediately in your book.
For transfers, take a screenshot of the successful payment or keep the bank alert.
Each month, keep paper receipts in one envelope marked with the month and year.
On your phone, keep receipt photos in an album with the month in its name.

blocks.title: What is not a business expense
blocks.text: School fees, household food, church or mosque offerings and personal clothing are not business expenses, even if you pay them from shop money. If you take money for these, record it as "owner's drawing" (lesson 3), not as an expense. Otherwise your profit figure becomes wrong.

If you buy something that lasts a long time for the business, such as a table, a freezer, a weighing scale or a sewing machine, write it on a separate **equipment** page with date and price. It is a business cost, but because it lasts for years, do not count the full price against one week's profit. Simply keep the record so you know what the business owns and what it cost.
Expenses you pay less often

Some costs come once a month or once a year: shop rent, association dues, a generator service, a trade fair stand. These are easy to forget when you look at one week, and then they arrive as a shock. Write a short list at the front of your expenses section of every cost that comes monthly or yearly, with the usual amount and the month it is due. Each week, set aside a small part toward them. For example, if stall rent is about ₦60,000 a year, putting aside about ₦1,200 a week (₦60,000 ÷ 52, rounded) means the rent is ready when it is due.

Watch prices too. When you record a stock purchase, write the quantity and the unit price, not only the total. Next time you buy, compare. If the price of a bag has gone up, you will see it the same day and can adjust your selling price before your profit disappears.
The aim is not perfect accounting. The aim is that when you ask "Where did my money go this month?", your expenses page answers in a few minutes.

takeaways: Separate stock purchases from running costs
Use about seven simple categories every week
Record small costs like levies, bags and bank charges
Keep receipts and screenshots by month
Household spending is a drawing, not a business expense

activity.title: Track one week of expenses
steps: Rule an expenses page with the six columns shown.
Record every business payment for one week.
Total the stock column and the running cost column separately.
Group running costs by category and circle the biggest one.
Write one idea to reduce your biggest running cost.
activity.evidence: Photo of the week's expenses page with totals and your category summary

lessons.title: The cash book: money in, money out, running balance
objectives: Keep a simple cash book with a running balance
Record opening balance, receipts and payments correctly
Check the book against cash in hand each day
Keep a separate column or book for bank and wallet money

blocks.text: The **cash book** is the record of every naira that comes in and goes out, in date order, with a **balance** after each line. The balance tells you how much money you should be holding right now. If you count your cash and it matches the balance, your records are right. If not, you know there is a mistake or a loss to find today, not in three months.

blocks.name: money-bag
blocks.caption: The cash book tells you how much should be in your money bag at any moment.

blocks.text: The simple cash book layout

Figures are illustrative. The rule for the balance is always the same: **previous balance + money in − money out = new balance**. Do it line by line. The closing balance of today becomes the opening balance of tomorrow.

blocks.title: Running balance rule
items: Previous balance
Add money in
Subtract money out
New balance
Count and compare
blocks.caption: Each line updates the balance, and at closing you compare it with what you count.

blocks.title: Worked example: checking Grace's cash book
blocks.context: For example, Grace sells provisions in Jos. Use the table above. Amounts are approximate.
steps: Opening: ₦15,000.
Grace counts her cash: ₦34,200. Difference: ₦35,000 − ₦34,200 = ₦800 short.
blocks.result: Grace's book says ₦35,000 but she holds ₦34,200. She writes "₦800 short" with the date, checks for an unrecorded expense, and remembers ₦800 she paid for sachet water for the shop. She adds that line and the book balances.

blocks.text: Cash and bank: two columns or two books

Most traders now receive money both as cash and into an account (bank, Moniepoint, Opay, PalmPay and others). Mixing them in one balance makes checking impossible, because you cannot count bank money with your hands. The simple solution is a **two-column cash book**: one set of In/Out/Balance columns for cash, another for bank or wallet. Check the cash balance by counting; check the bank balance against your app.

When you move money between them, such as depositing cash at a POS agent into your account, write it as **cash out** and **bank in** on the same line. It is not a sale or an expense, just money changing pockets. Also record any agent or bank charge as an expense.

blocks.title: Count your float
blocks.text: Start each day with a fixed amount of change (the float), for example ₦5,000 in small notes. Write it as the opening cash. This makes counting at night easier and stops you from mixing yesterday's money with today's.

blocks.title: Keep cash safe
blocks.text: Do not keep large amounts of cash in the stall overnight. Deposit extra cash into your account regularly, and do not count large sums openly in the market. A record of cash is only useful if the cash is still there.
Common cash book mistakes

items: Forgetting the opening balance, so every balance after it is wrong.
Adding money out instead of subtracting it.
Writing a credit sale as money in. Credit is not cash until the customer pays.
Writing a stock purchase in the cash book but not in the expenses page or stock card.
Waiting until the end of the week to write everything from memory.

blocks.text: A good habit is to draw a line under each day, write the closing balance, and count your cash before you leave the market. It takes five minutes. When you find a mistake on the same day, you still remember what happened. After a week, nobody remembers.

Some traders also keep a small **petty cash** envelope for tiny daily costs like sachet water, a pen or a small tip for loaders. Put a fixed amount in it, for example ₦3,000, write each small payment on a slip inside, and when it runs low, total the slips, record them as expenses and refill the envelope. Your main cash book then shows one clear line instead of many tiny ones.

If you get a difference that you cannot explain after checking, do not change the balance to make it look right. Write a line called "Cash short" or "Cash over" with the amount. Over a month, these lines tell you whether you have a small, normal error rate or a real problem.

takeaways: Previous balance + in − out = new balance, line by line
Count cash daily and compare with the balance
Keep separate columns for cash and bank or wallet
Moving cash to the bank is not a sale or expense
Write unexplained differences as cash short or over

activity.title: Balance your cash book for three days
steps: Count your cash and write it as the opening balance.
Record every money in and money out with a running balance.
At closing, count your cash and compare with the book.
Do the same for your bank or wallet using your app.
Write any differences and what you found.
activity.evidence: Three days of cash book pages showing balances, counts and any differences explained

lessons.title: Separating business money from personal money
objectives: Explain why mixing business and household money hides losses
Set a fixed weekly amount to pay yourself
Record owner's drawings in your cash book
Use a separate account or wallet for business money

blocks.text: For many women traders, the shop money and the house money live in the same purse. School fees come from today's sales. Soup ingredients come from the shelf. Money for a relative's emergency comes from the drawer. This is understandable, because the business exists to feed the family. But when the two are mixed without records, you cannot tell if the business is making money, and the capital slowly disappears.

blocks.name: savings
blocks.alt: A person putting money into savings
blocks.caption: Keeping business money apart from household money protects the capital that keeps you trading.

blocks.text: The idea of paying yourself

Think of the business as a separate person who employs you. The business pays you a fixed amount each week, your **salary** or **drawing**. You use that money for the house. Everything else stays in the business to buy stock and pay costs. If the business cannot afford your drawing, your records will show it, and you can act before the shop collapses.

blocks.title: Mixed purse versus separate money
items: Mixed purse
Separate money
blocks.caption: Separating money does not mean less for the family; it means you know what the business can really afford.
left: Hard to show a lender anything
right: Records ready for loans and partners

blocks.text: Recording drawings

Whenever you take money or goods out of the business for personal use, write it in the cash book as money out with the word **Drawing**. If you take goods, write them in the stock card Out column at the price you paid, with the note "home use", and write them as a drawing too. Drawings are **not** business expenses. They come out of profit, not before it.

blocks.title: Worked example: how much can Joy pay herself?
blocks.context: For example, Joy sells cooked food. Over four weeks her records show the following. Amounts are approximate.
steps: Average weekly sales: about ₦120,000.
Average weekly food stock (ingredients): about ₦72,000.
Average weekly running costs (gas, transport, packs, levy): about ₦18,000.
She decides to pay herself ₦20,000 a week and leave ₦10,000 in the business to grow and to cover slow weeks.
blocks.result: Joy's fixed drawing is ₦20,000 a week. Her household budget is planned around it, and the business keeps about ₦10,000 a week to build up stock and savings.

blocks.text: Practical ways to keep money apart

items: Open a separate account or wallet just for the business. Many banks and wallet providers offer simple accounts you can open from your phone; ask them what documents they need.
Ask customers to transfer only to the business account.
Keep business cash in a separate purse, box or envelope from your personal money.
Pay yourself on the same day every week by transfer or cash, and record it as a Drawing.
If an emergency forces you to take extra, write it as a Drawing too, and plan to put it back if you can.

blocks.title: Family requests
blocks.text: When relatives ask for money from the shop, a written record helps. You can show that the business has a fixed amount for the household and that extra withdrawals reduce the money for restocking. This turns a hard conversation into a practical one.
What happens to profit you do not draw

Profit you leave in the business becomes more **capital**: more stock, a better stall, money for a slow season. Over months, that is how a small business grows. If you draw every naira of profit, the business stays the same size. If you draw more than the profit, it shrinks. Your cash book and drawings record make this visible.
Your own goods and your own labour

Remember that your time has value too. If you work twelve hours a day in the shop and the business makes ₦30,000 profit a week, that profit is really your pay for those hours. Comparing it honestly with what you could earn doing something else helps you decide whether to grow, change products or change how you work. Records give you the numbers to make that choice calmly. Also be careful not to lend business money to friends from the shop drawer without writing it. A loan to a friend is not a drawing and not an expense; write it on its own page as money owed to the business, with a date for repayment.

Start with a drawing you can sustain, based on at least four weeks of records. Review it every month: raise it when profit grows, lower it in a slow season. The key is that it is a decision you make with numbers, not a guess.

takeaways: Mixing money hides whether the business is profitable
Pay yourself a fixed weekly drawing
Record money and goods taken as Drawing, not expense
Use a separate business account or wallet
Profit left in the business grows your capital

objectives: Combine sales, expenses and drawings into one weekly summary
Produce a monthly summary from weekly figures
Check that the summary agrees with your cash and bank balances
Use the summary to plan next month

blocks.text: You now have several records: sales, expenses, stock, debtors and the cash book. A **money summary** brings their totals together on one page. A weekly summary takes about fifteen minutes. A monthly summary takes about thirty. Together they give you a clear view of your business that most small traders never have.

blocks.name: bar-chart
blocks.caption: A weekly summary turns many records into a few numbers you can compare.

blocks.text: The weekly money summary

head: Item
Amount (₦)
Where it comes from
rows: Cash and bank at week end

blocks.text: These figures are illustrative and approximate. This page does not calculate profit yet; that needs the stock count too, which you will learn in Module 4. It shows the money flows: what came in, what went out, and where the rest is.

items: Daily: write and check
Saturday: weekly summary
Month end: add weeks
Month end: count stock
Plan next month
blocks.caption: Each step uses the one before it, so the monthly view is only as good as the daily writing.

blocks.text: Checking the summary

A useful check: **opening cash and bank + cash sales and transfer sales + debts collected − all payments out = closing cash and bank**. If your weekly summary and cash book agree, you can trust both. If not, go back to the days of the week and find the gap. Usually it is a missed expense or a sale written in the wrong column.

blocks.title: Worked example: Halima checks her week
blocks.context: For example, Halima's week. Amounts are approximate.
steps: Opening cash and bank on Monday: ₦30,000.
Money received: cash sales ₦106,000 + transfers ₦70,000 + debts collected ₦3,000 = ₦179,000.
Money paid out: stock ₦110,000 + running costs ₦17,700 + drawings ₦20,000 = ₦147,700.
Her counted cash plus bank app balance on Saturday night: ₦61,300.
blocks.result: The week balances exactly. Halima can trust her records, and she knows ₦61,300 is available, ₦12,000 is still with debtors, and her shelves hold the stock she bought.

blocks.text: The monthly summary

At month end, add the four or five weekly summaries into one monthly table: total sales, total stock bought, total running costs (by category), total drawings, debtors at month end, and cash and bank at month end. Add the stock count value at cost from your stock cards. Write two or three sentences: what went well, what went badly, what you will change.

items: Did sales go up or down compared with last month? Why?
Which running cost category grew the most?
Did debtors grow? Who is late?
Did you draw more than you planned?
Is there enough money to restock fully next week?

blocks.title: Make it a ritual
blocks.text: Choose the last Saturday or Sunday of each month. Sit with your records, a calculator and a cup of tea for half an hour. Treat it like a meeting with your business.
Planning with the summary

Use the monthly summary to plan. If you know festive season sales usually rise, plan to buy more stock and set money aside beforehand. If a running cost keeps growing, look for a cheaper option. If debtors are rising, tighten your credit rules. The summary turns your records from a diary of the past into a tool for the future.

blocks.title: Worked example: planning for a festive month
blocks.context: For example, Halima's monthly summaries show that December sales are much higher than November. Amounts are approximate.
steps: Last November her stock purchases were about ₦440,000.
Last December she ran out of her top products in the second week and lost sales.
This year she plans to buy about ₦600,000 of stock for December.
That is ₦600,000 − ₦440,000 = ₦160,000 more than a normal month.
From October she sets aside about ₦20,000 a week for eight weeks: 8 × ₦20,000 = ₦160,000.
blocks.result: Because her records showed the December pattern, Halima saves the ₦160,000 extra stock money in advance instead of borrowing at the last minute.

blocks.text: If your monthly summary shows less money than you expected, do not panic. Check three things in order: did stock on the shelf grow (money turned into goods), did debtors grow (money still with customers), or did drawings grow (money taken home)? One of these usually explains most of the gap, and each has a clear fix.

Keep your monthly summaries together, at the back of your notebook or in a separate folder. After six or twelve months, you will have something very valuable: a clear history of your business that you can show a lender, a cooperative or a partner, and that you can learn from yourself.

takeaways: One page brings all records together each week
Opening + money in − money out = closing; check it
Add weeks into a monthly summary with stock value
Write a few sentences of what you learned each month
Keep summaries together as your business history

modules.title: Using records to grow your business
modules.overview: Records only pay off when you use them. This module shows you how to read your records for warning signs and opportunities, calculate profit properly with stock, prepare a simple record pack for loans, grants and partners, and move your records onto a phone safely.

lessons.title: Reading your records: what the numbers are telling you
objectives: Ask five key questions of your records each month
Calculate a simple markup and margin for a product
Spot warning signs in sales, stock, debtors and cash
Turn one finding into a specific action

blocks.text: Writing records every day is the hard part. Reading them is the rewarding part. Once a month, sit with your summaries and ask questions. Each question has an answer somewhere in your books, and each answer suggests something to do.

blocks.name: data-analysis
blocks.caption: Reading your records means asking questions and finding the answers in your own numbers.

blocks.text: Five questions to ask every month

head: Question
Where to look
What to do with the answer
rows: Are sales going up or down?
Find the reason: season, price, competitor, location
Which products make the most money?
Sales by product and purchase prices
Stock more of them, give them the best space
Tighten checks, fix storage, talk to helpers
Chase old debts, tighten credit rules
Is there enough cash to restock?
Adjust drawings, plan purchases, save ahead

blocks.title: Which products deserve your money?
items: Sells fast, good profit
Sells fast, low profit
Sells slowly, good profit
Sells slowly, low profit
blocks.caption: Put each product in a box: keep the top left well stocked, review prices for the top right, keep small quantities of the bottom left, and consider dropping the bottom right.

blocks.text: Profit per item: markup and margin

For each main product you need two numbers: what you **pay** for it (cost price) and what you **sell** it for (selling price). The difference is your **gross profit per item**. Traders talk about this in two ways. **Markup** compares profit with the cost price. **Margin** compares profit with the selling price. They are easy to mix up, so use one consistently.

blocks.title: Worked example: Ifeoma's two products
blocks.context: For example, Ifeoma sells household goods in Onitsha. Prices are approximate.
steps: Detergent pack: costs ₦1,500, sells for ₦1,800. Profit per pack: ₦300. Markup: ₦300 ÷ ₦1,500 = 0.20, so 20%. Margin: ₦300 ÷ ₦1,800 = about 0.17, so about 17%.
Plastic bowl set: costs ₦4,000, sells for ₦6,000. Profit per set: ₦2,000. Markup: ₦2,000 ÷ ₦4,000 = 50%. Margin: ₦2,000 ÷ ₦6,000 = about 33%.
From her product count, she sells about 60 detergent packs a week and 5 bowl sets.
Weekly profit from detergent: 60 × ₦300 = ₦18,000. From bowls: 5 × ₦2,000 = ₦10,000.
blocks.result: The bowls have the higher margin, but detergent brings more total profit because it sells fast. Ifeoma keeps detergent always in stock and displays the bowls better to sell more of them.

blocks.text: Warning signs to watch

items: Sales falling for two or more months in a row without a clear reason.
Cash shortages appearing most days, not just occasionally.
Stock gaps growing every week.
Debts older than four weeks increasing.
Your weekly drawing larger than your weekly profit.
Supplier prices rising while your selling prices stay the same.

blocks.title: One finding, one action
blocks.text: Do not try to fix everything at once. Each month, choose the single most important finding and decide one clear action with a date, for example: "From Monday, no new credit to anyone owing more than two weeks." Write it at the top of next month's page and check it at month end.
Comparing over time

A single month tells you little. Patterns appear when you compare: this month with last month, this December with last December, this week with the same week last month. Many traders notice that sales follow the calendar: school resumption, salary week at month end, festive seasons, rainy season. Once you see your own pattern in your own records, you can buy stock before the busy period and keep costs low in the slow period.

Also compare your records with your feelings. Many traders feel that a product is their best seller because customers ask about it often. The records may show something else. Trust the numbers, but use your experience to explain them. The best decisions come from both together.
Turning a finding into a price decision

Records also help you set prices. When a supplier raises the cost of an item, check your margin. If detergent rises from ₦1,500 to ₦1,650 and you still sell at ₦1,800, your profit per pack falls from ₦300 to ₦150, half of what it was. At 60 packs a week, that is ₦9,000 less profit every week. You might raise your price a little, look for another supplier, or accept a smaller margin on purpose to keep customers. The record does not decide for you, but it shows you exactly what each choice costs.

Look at your running costs as a share of sales too. If transport is ₦9,000 out of ₦150,000 weekly sales, that is about 6 naira in every 100. If it rises to 10 naira in every 100, it is time to look for a cheaper way to move goods.
Finally, share what you learn with someone you trust: a fellow trader, a cooperative leader, a WODDI mentor. Explaining your numbers out loud often helps you see what to do next.

takeaways: Ask five questions each month: sales, products, stock, debts, cash
Know cost price, selling price and profit per item
A fast seller with low margin can earn more than a slow seller with high margin
Pick one finding and one dated action each month
Compare months and seasons to find your pattern

lessons.title: Calculating profit or loss simply and correctly
objectives: Calculate cost of goods sold using opening stock, purchases and closing stock
Work out gross profit and net profit for a month
Explain why cash in hand is not the same as profit
Include bad debts and owner's drawings correctly

blocks.text: **Profit** is what the business earns after paying for the goods it sold and all its running costs. A **loss** is when costs are bigger than sales. To calculate it properly for a month, you need four records: your sales total, your stock purchases, your stock count at the start and end of the month, and your running costs.

blocks.name: chart-with-upwards-trend
blocks.caption: Profit is what remains after the cost of goods sold and running costs.

blocks.text: Why stock counts matter

If you buy ₦400,000 of goods this month but sell only part of them, it is wrong to count the whole ₦400,000 against this month's sales. The unsold goods are still on your shelf and still have value. So you calculate the **cost of goods sold**, the cost of only what actually left the shop.

blocks.title: From sales to net profit
items: Sales
Minus cost of goods sold
Gross profit
Minus running costs
Net profit
blocks.caption: Each step removes one kind of cost until only true profit remains.

blocks.text: The three formulas

items: **Cost of goods sold** = opening stock (at cost) + stock purchases − closing stock (at cost).
**Gross profit** = sales − cost of goods sold.
**Net profit** = gross profit − running costs (transport, rent, levies, packaging, phone, staff, charges, bad debts).

blocks.text: Value stock at what you **paid**, not at your selling price. Count sales as all goods sold this month, including credit sales. If a debt becomes clearly unrecoverable, count it as a running cost called **bad debt**. Your drawings are **not** a running cost; they come out of net profit afterwards.

blocks.title: Worked example: Halima's October profit
blocks.context: For example, Halima's provisions stall. All amounts are approximate.
steps: Sales for October (cash, transfer and credit): ₦744,000.
Opening stock on 1 October, counted and valued at cost: ₦150,000.
Stock purchases in October: ₦520,000.
Closing stock on 31 October, at cost: ₦170,000.
Running costs: transport ₦36,000 + levy ₦7,200 + packaging ₦9,600 + phone ₦6,000 + helper ₦12,000 + bank and POS charges ₦3,200 + one bad debt ₦4,000 = ₦78,000.
blocks.result: Halima's net profit for October is about ₦166,000. She drew ₦80,000 during the month, so about ₦86,000 stayed in the business as extra capital.

blocks.text: Profit versus cash

Your profit and the change in your cash will rarely be the same. In Halima's month, stock on the shelf grew by ₦20,000 (from ₦150,000 to ₦170,000), which used cash but is not a cost. Customers may owe more at the end than at the start, which counts as sales but is not yet cash. This is why a trader can be profitable and still short of cash, or have plenty of cash while making a loss. You need both the profit calculation and the cash book.

head: Situation
Profit
Cash
rows: You buy extra stock before a festive season
You sell a lot on credit

blocks.title: Do not skip the stock count
blocks.text: Without opening and closing stock values, you can only estimate profit from sales minus purchases, and that can be badly wrong in months when you buy a lot or very little stock. Count your main products at month end, even if quickly.
A quick daily estimate

Between month ends you can estimate profit roughly from your markup. If your average margin is about 33% (a third of the selling price is profit) and you sold ₦30,000 today, your gross profit today is roughly ₦10,000, before running costs. Use this for quick decisions, and the full monthly calculation for the real answer.
Writing a simple profit statement

Put your monthly profit on one neat page with these lines in order: Sales; Opening stock; Add purchases; Less closing stock; Cost of goods sold; Gross profit; then each running cost category; Total running costs; Net profit. Underneath, write Drawings and Profit kept in the business. This one page, kept every month, is the document lenders and partners find most useful, and it takes only a few minutes once your other records are in order.

If your calculation shows a loss, do not hide it. Look at which line is the problem: sales too low, cost of goods too high (prices or missing stock), or running costs too high. Each has a different fix, and your other records tell you which.

takeaways: Cost of goods sold = opening stock + purchases − closing stock
Gross profit = sales − cost of goods sold
Net profit = gross profit − running costs
Value stock at cost; drawings are not a cost
Profit and cash are different; you need both records
