lessons.title: Records for loans, grants and business partners
objectives: List the records lenders, grant programmes and partners commonly ask for
Prepare a simple business record pack
Judge whether you can afford a loan repayment from your records
Recognise and avoid loan scams

blocks.text: When you apply for a loan from a cooperative, microfinance bank or bank, or for a grant or training programme, or when a supplier or partner considers working with you, they want to know one thing: **is this business real, steady and able to pay?** Your records answer that question better than any talk.

blocks.name: business-deal
blocks.alt: Two people agreeing a business deal
blocks.caption: Clear records help a lender or partner trust your business.

blocks.text: What is commonly asked

items: Your sales over recent months, ideally monthly summaries.
Bank or wallet statements showing money flowing through the business.
A simple profit calculation for recent months.
A list of what the business owns (stock value, equipment) and what it owes (supplier credit, other loans).
Basic business details: name, location, what you sell, how long you have traded.
Identification and, for registered businesses, registration documents from the Corporate Affairs Commission (CAC).

blocks.text: Every lender and programme has its own requirements, so always ask for their exact list before you apply. The point of this lesson is that if you have kept the records in this course, most of what they ask for is already in your notebook.

blocks.title: Your business record pack
items: Monthly sales summaries
Bank or wallet statements
Profit calculations
Stock and equipment list
Debts owed and owing
blocks.caption: Five items, kept up to date in one folder, prepare you for most loan or partner conversations.

blocks.text: Can you afford the repayment?

Before you borrow, use your own records to check that the business can repay from **profit**, not from capital. A loan used to buy stock should increase sales and profit by more than the repayment, otherwise it makes you poorer.

blocks.title: Worked example: should Esther take this loan?
blocks.context: For example, Esther's drinks business is offered a loan with a monthly repayment. Amounts are approximate.
steps: Her records show average monthly net profit of about ₦120,000.
Her monthly drawing for the household is ₦80,000.
Profit left after drawing: ₦120,000 − ₦80,000 = ₦40,000 a month.
The loan repayment would be ₦55,000 a month.
₦55,000 is more than ₦40,000, so she is short by ₦15,000 every month unless the loan raises her profit by at least that much.
blocks.result: Esther asks for a smaller loan or a longer period, or plans exactly how the extra stock will raise profit by more than ₦15,000 a month, before she signs anything.

blocks.title: Avoid loan scams
blocks.text: Never pay a "processing fee" to someone who calls or messages you offering a loan or grant. Never share your BVN, card PIN or one-time codes with anyone. Before using a loan app, check that it appears on the list of approved digital lenders published by the Federal Competition and Consumer Protection Commission (FCCPC). Read the total amount you will repay, not only the monthly figure.
Grants and programmes

Grant and support programmes for small businesses and women entrepreneurs appear from time to time, run by government, development agencies, banks and non-profits. Application forms often ask for monthly sales, number of customers or how you will use the money. Answer only with figures from your records, and keep a copy of what you submitted. Be wary of any "grant" that asks you to pay first.
Telling your business story with numbers

When you speak to a lender or a programme, use your records to tell a short, clear story: what you sell, for how long, your average monthly sales, your typical monthly profit, and exactly how the money would be used and how it would increase profit. For example: "I sell provisions in the same market. My average sales over six months are about ₦700,000 a month and net profit about ₦150,000. With ₦300,000 more stock before December I expect higher festive sales, based on last December's records." Figures from your own books are far more convincing than promises.
Partners and suppliers

A supplier deciding whether to give you goods on credit, or a person considering joining your business, will trust records they can see. Show them your monthly summaries and your history of paying suppliers on time from your creditors page. If you go into partnership, agree in writing how profit will be shared and how records will be kept, and give each partner access to the books.

items: Make a folder (paper or a phone folder) called "Business record pack".
Put in your last three to six monthly summaries and profit calculations.
Add bank or wallet statements for the same months (most apps let you download one).
Add a one-page list of stock value, equipment, and debts owed and owing.
Update it at the end of every month.

lessons.title: Moving from paper to phone records
objectives: Set up a simple sales and cash sheet in Google Sheets
Use SUM and a running balance formula
Judge whether a bookkeeping app is suitable and safe
Back up phone records and protect your data

blocks.text: Once your paper habit is steady, a phone can save time and reduce adding mistakes. You do not need to stop using paper. Many traders write in a notebook during the day and type the totals into a phone at night. This lesson shows you a free spreadsheet method using **Google Sheets**, and what to check before trusting any bookkeeping app.

blocks.name: spreadsheets
blocks.alt: A person working with a spreadsheet
blocks.caption: A free spreadsheet on your phone can add up your records for you.

blocks.text: Getting started with Google Sheets

items: Install the Google Sheets app from the Play Store or App Store and sign in with a Google (Gmail) account.
Tap the + button to create a new blank spreadsheet. Name it, for example "Shop records 2026".
In row 1, type the headings: Date, Details, Money in, Money out, Balance.
From row 2, type one line per day or per transaction, the same as your cash book.
Your work saves automatically to your Google account when you have data.

blocks.text: A **spreadsheet** is a grid of boxes called **cells**. Columns have letters (A, B, C) and rows have numbers (1, 2, 3). So the cell in column C, row 2 is called **C2**. Formulas start with an equals sign and do the adding for you.
Two formulas that do most of the work

head: What you want
Formula
Where to type it
rows: E3, then copy it down the column
Total money in for the month
Under the last row of column C
Total money out for the month
Under the last row of column D

blocks.text: The running balance formula means: previous balance, plus money in on this row, minus money out on this row. When you copy it down, the spreadsheet adjusts the row numbers automatically. The SUM formula adds every cell from C2 to C40. Change 40 to your last row.

blocks.title: From notebook to phone
items: Write in notebook
Total at closing
Type totals into sheet
Formulas update balance
Check against cash
blocks.caption: The notebook stays your original record; the phone does the adding and keeps a backup.

blocks.title: Worked example: Kemi types a week into Sheets
blocks.context: For example, Kemi types her daily bread totals each night. Amounts are approximate.
steps: E2: opening balance 10000.
Row 3: Monday, sales in C3 = 32600, flour and costs out D3 = 24000. E3 shows 10000 + 32600 − 24000 = 18600.
She counts her cash and app balance: ₦31,600 together.
blocks.result: The sheet matches her count, and she did not need to add a single number by hand. At month end, the SUM formulas give her total money in and out instantly.

blocks.text: Choosing a bookkeeping app

There are also free and paid bookkeeping apps made for small businesses, including some built for Nigerian traders. Apps come and go, so instead of trusting a name, check these points before you put your business records in one:

items: Is it free, or is the price clear and affordable?
Does it work offline when your data is finished or the network is poor?
Can you export or download your records (for example as a spreadsheet or PDF)?
Does it have many recent good reviews in the Play Store or App Store?
Does it ask for permissions it does not need, such as your contacts or photos, for no clear reason?
If it offers loans, is the lender on the FCCPC approved list?

blocks.title: Protect your records and your money
blocks.text: Lock your phone with a PIN or fingerprint. Never share your Google password or one-time codes. Do not keep bank PINs or passwords in your spreadsheet. If several people need access, share the sheet only with people you trust, and you can give them view-only access.
Backing up

Google Sheets keeps your file in your Google account, so if your phone is lost you can sign in on a new phone and find it. For apps, check whether backup is automatic or something you must switch on. For paper records, take a photo of each completed page every week and keep the photos in a dedicated album or folder. A record you cannot find after a theft or a flood is no record at all.

A good weekly routine on the phone: on Saturday evening, check that every day of the week has a row, that the last balance matches your counted cash and app balance, and that the SUM totals agree with your weekly summary in the notebook. If they disagree, the mistake is usually a number typed wrongly, such as 3,260 instead of 32,600. Looking for a difference that is exactly divisible by 9 often points to two digits swapped, for example 2,850 typed as 2,580.
Move slowly. Start with one sheet, the cash book, for a month. When you are comfortable, add a sales summary tab and a debtors tab. The aim is records you trust and use, not the most advanced system.

takeaways: Keep paper as your original record; use the phone for totals and backup
Cells are named by column letter and row number
Running balance: =previous balance + in − out
SUM adds a column for you
Check any app for offline use, export, reviews and safe permissions

Ask for a smaller loan or longer period, or show how profit will rise by at least ₦15,000
Pay the repayment from her capital
quiz.explain: Repayments should come from profit. She is ₦15,000 short monthly unless the loan raises profit by at least that much.

quiz.q: Someone calls offering a grant if Halima first pays a ₦10,000 processing fee. What should she do?
options: Refuse; genuine programmes do not ask you to pay first by phone
Ask a friend to pay it
quiz.explain: Upfront fee requests by phone or message are a common scam. Never pay or share BVN, PIN or codes.

quiz.q: In Google Sheets, E2 holds the opening balance, C3 money in and D3 money out. Which formula gives the balance in E3?
quiz.explain: New balance = previous balance + money in − money out, so =E2+C3-D3.

finalQuiz.q: Which statement about money in your bag at the end of the day is correct?
options: It includes money needed to restock and pay costs
It is only the money from credit sales
It equals your net profit for the month
finalQuiz.explain: Cash in hand includes capital for new stock and money for costs. Profit is only what is left after those.

finalQuiz.q: A customer buys goods on credit. Which records change?
finalQuiz.explain: The sale happened and the goods left, so sales and stock change; no cash came, so it goes in the debtors list.

finalQuiz.q: Kemi sells 20 small loaves at ₦700 and 10 big loaves at ₦1,500. What are her total sales?
A trader starts the week with 12 cartons, buys 20, and counts 9 at the end. Her sales book shows 21 sold. What does this show?
finalQuiz.explain: 12 + 20 − 9 = 23 cartons left the shop, but only 21 were recorded as sold, so 2 are unexplained.

finalQuiz.q: Which debt should a trader chase first?
options: The oldest debt past its promised date
The debt of her best friend
finalQuiz.explain: The longer a debt stays unpaid, the harder it is to collect, so older overdue debts come first.

finalQuiz.q: Which of these is a running cost?
options: A bag of rice bought for resale
Cash deposited at a POS agent
finalQuiz.explain: Market levy is a cost of trading. Rice for resale is stock, school fees are a drawing, and a deposit just moves money.

finalQuiz.q: Opening cash ₦8,000. Money in ₦30,000. Money out ₦21,500. What should the closing balance be?
A trader's average weekly profit is ₦25,000. Which weekly drawing lets the business grow?
finalQuiz.explain: Only a drawing below profit leaves money in the business to build capital. ₦18,000 leaves about ₦7,000 a week.

finalQuiz.q: A product costs ₦4,000 and sells for ₦6,000. What is the margin on the selling price?
finalQuiz.explain: Margin = profit ÷ selling price = ₦2,000 ÷ ₦6,000, about 33%. (Markup on cost would be 50%.)

finalQuiz.q: Opening stock ₦100,000, purchases ₦300,000, closing stock ₦120,000, sales ₦400,000, running costs ₦50,000. What is net profit?
A message offers a business grant if you send ₦5,000 and your BVN today. What should you do?
options: Ignore or report it; never pay upfront or share BVN, PIN or codes
Ask the sender for a discount
finalQuiz.explain: Upfront fees and requests for BVN or codes are signs of a scam.

finalQuiz.q: In Google Sheets, which formula adds all money in from C2 to C31?
finalQuiz.explain: SUM with a range (C2:C31) adds every cell from C2 to C31. C2+C31 adds only two cells.

capstone.title: One-month business record portfolio
capstone.brief: Keep complete records of your own business for four weeks and produce a portfolio: daily sales and cash pages, expenses, stock cards for your top products, a debtors list, weekly and monthly summaries, a monthly profit statement, your drawing plan and a short record pack ready for a lender or partner.
steps: Set up your notebook (or picture book) with the five sections and count your opening cash, bank balance and stock.
Record every sale, expense, credit sale and payment daily, and balance your cash book each evening.
Every Saturday, count your top products, update stock cards, sort debtors by age and write the weekly summary.
At month end, count and value stock at cost and write your monthly summary.
Calculate cost of goods sold, gross profit and net profit, and compare net profit with your drawings.
Answer the five monthly questions and choose one action with a date.
Assemble your record pack and, if you like, copy your cash book into Google Sheets.
evidence: Photos of at least 20 days of sales and cash book pages with daily balances
Expenses pages with weekly totals by category
Stock cards for at least three products with weekly counts
Debtors list sorted by age with credit rules written
Four weekly summaries and one monthly summary with balance check
One-page profit statement with every formula shown
Written drawing amount and record of actual drawings
Record pack folder and one dated action from your monthly review
